misconceptions.correction: It evidences a specified disposal event; scope must be checked against replicas, backups, exports, and holds.

misconceptions.correction: The hold applies to identified scope and relevant preservation duties, not unrelated data.

outcome: Choose a retention decision and disposal method for an asset while accounting for legal holds, media, replicas, and evidence.

sections.body: Retention schedules identify the record class, owner, minimum and maximum period where applicable, trigger, storage and access requirements, and disposition authority. Inputs include business usefulness, contractual commitments, regulation, litigation or investigation needs, privacy principles, cost, and risk. A legal hold or investigation suspends ordinary disposition for the affected scope.
keyPoints: A retention trigger might be contract end, case close, employee departure, or transaction completion.
Legal holds override routine destruction until released by the responsible authority.
Retention applies across systems and copies that fall within scope.
sections.title: Set a defensible retention rule

sections.body: Data remanence is recoverable residual information left after ordinary deletion or incomplete sanitization. Select an approved sanitization method for the actual medium, information sensitivity, intended reuse, and acceptable recovery effort. Clear, purge, and destroy describe sanitization methods; cryptographic erase is a technique whose suitability depends on the encryption implementation and the ability to sanitize every relevant key. Ordinary file deletion or a generic overwrite rule is not enough for every medium. Preserve custody and account for scoped replicas and backups. Verification checks that the technique completed as expected; validation uses that evidence, the method’s suitability, and relevant anomalies to decide whether the result is acceptable. If it is not, keep custody and repeat or escalate the method before releasing the media.
keyPoints: Disposal is a process with authorization, execution, verification, and evidence.
Different media and encryption states change the appropriate sanitization method.
Destroying a server does not automatically destroy replicated cloud or backup data.
sections.title: Make disposal effective and provable

sections.body: Vendor end-of-life (EOL) announcements describe product discontinuation milestones, while end of support (EOS) identifies the loss of specified maintenance or assistance. Exact labels and support entitlements depend on the vendor notice and contract. These milestones trigger an organization’s own migration, continued-use risk decision, or retirement/decommissioning plan; they are not automatically the date the organization removes the asset. Identify dependent data and services, readable export formats, migration or compensating-control needs, license effects, owner approval, and disposal evidence. A legal hold may require preserving records but does not itself authorize indefinite operation of unsupported technology.
keyPoints: Unsupported software and hardware can make ordinary retention or continued operation unsafe.
Retirement planning includes data export, access revocation, keys, dependencies, contracts, and evidence.
Exceptions need scope, owner, expiry, compensating controls, and reassessment.
sections.title: Treat end of life and end of support as retention decisions
